source.title: Weed Out, Then Harvest: Dual Low-Rank Adaptation is an Effective Noisy Label Detector for Noise-Robust Learning
source.authors: Bo Yuan; Yu-Lin Chen; Yin Zhang

record.tranche_reason: Tests the training-time memorization pattern on text classification with a language model and LoRA modules, extending the cited memory-effect work to this setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own memorization results in Figure 3 for Trec under 20%A. Results on noisy-label detection and test accuracy do not report training error on completely random labels, convergence time, unstructured inputs, or training error across noise levels, so they do not test V1–V5. Cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Section 5.5 reports that the baseline without noise handling learns clean samples before gradually fitting noisy samples, testing V6 in language-model fine-tuning. Delora's deliberately constrained modules do not independently test that spontaneous learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the Figure 3 analysis: the baseline learns clean samples before noisy ones, while constrained LoRAs specialize in different sample types. The paper's broader conclusion is that decoupling noisy-label detection from classifier training improves noise detection and text classification across tested datasets and backbones.
record.recipe_differences: Measures sample memorization during noisy-label text classification fine-tuning; uses LLaMA-based LoRA modules and a 20%A setting rather than the original study's image-classification experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported memorization analysis is limited to Trec under 20%A; the base model and the deliberately constrained clean/noisy LoRAs show different patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Delora's clean and noisy LoRAs preferentially memorize their assigned sample types under deliberately different parameter-update constraints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic constraints can induce separate LoRA modules to specialize in clean and noisy samples during noisy-label fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2025
record.problems: The memorization evidence is limited to one dataset and one noise setting; Figure 3 provides the ratios without numeric values in the text or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were identified. Other tables report noisy-label detection precision/recall or test accuracy, not the training-time or random-label behaviors named in V1–V5.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across corruption fractions and steady test-error degradation through completely random labels. Test accuracies at selected noise levels do not establish this joint claim.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and generalization with true labels.
Fully random labels and learning dynamics outside the baseline Trec 20% asymmetric-noise setting; direct separation of shared-pattern learning from individual-example memorization.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the proposed V6 limits_scope verdict for R3–R6: intentionally induced specialization is not a boundary condition on spontaneous clean-first learning. The supplied text identifies the backbone and LoRA fine-tuning setup, but does not provide readable Figure 3 curve values or uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence as the corrupted-label fraction changes.
Perfect training fit and test error across corruption fractions through all-random labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
The study tests noisy text labels, not completely random labels; it reports qualitative training-time ratios, not numeric rates.
